title: Problem Solving: Flowcharts & Pseudocode Made Simple
subtitle: ISO Shape Reference Guide, Precision Vector Flowcharts & Execution Trace Tables
content:
What is an Algorithm? Think of a Recipe!

Before you bake a cake, you need a recipe. If a recipe says "mix stuff and bake until it looks ready," that's a terrible recipe because it is vague and ambiguous. But if it says:
 1. Take 2 eggs and 1 cup of flour
 2. Whisk for 3 minutes until smooth
 3. Bake at 350°F for exactly 25 minutes
Anyone following that recipe will produce the exact same delicious cake! In computer science, an Algorithm is precisely that: a finite, unambiguous, step-by-step procedure to solve a specific problem.

The 4 Non-Negotiable Rules of Every Valid Algorithm (Slide 31)

• Clear & Unambiguous: Every single instruction must have only one possible interpretation.
• Well-Defined Inputs & Outputs: Accepts zero or more defined inputs and guarantees one or more defined outputs.
• Finiteness (Must Terminate!): Must stop executing after a countable, finite number of steps. An infinite loop is never an algorithm!
• Language-Independent: Stated in pure mathematical and logical terms so it can be implemented in C, Python, Java, or Rust alike.

Pseudocode: The Rosetta Stone Between Thought and C

Trying to design algorithm logic while simultaneously worrying about semicolons, curly braces, and compiler errors causes cognitive overload. Pseudocode bridges this gap—it is structured English that mirrors high-level code structure without strict syntax penalties.

1. Human Thought
"Ask the user for four exam marks. Find their average. If the average is below 40, they failed; otherwise they passed."
2. Clean Pseudocode
READ m1, m2, m3, m4
avg = (m1 + m2 + m3 + m4) / 4

IF avg < 40 THEN
    PRINT "Fail"
ELSE
    PRINT "Pass"
ENDIF
3. Actual C Language
float m1, m2, m3, m4, avg;
scanf("%f %f %f %f", &m1, &m2, &m3, &m4);
avg = (m1 + m2 + m3 + m4) / 4.0;

if (avg < 40) {
    printf("Fail\n");
} else {
    printf("Pass\n");
}

Standard ISO Flowchart Shapes: Geometric Reference Guide

A Flowchart is a formalized diagrammatic representation of an algorithm using standardized geometric symbols (ISO 5807). Each shape has an unambiguous mathematical role:

Terminal Symbol
Oval / Stadium / Capsule
Marks the absolute entry point (START) or exit point (STOP / END) of the program. Every flowchart must have at least one.
Real Example: START or STOP
C Equivalent: int main(void) { ... return 0; }
Input / Output Symbol
True Angled Parallelogram
Used whenever the program receives external data from the user/keyboard (READ) or presents answers on the screen (PRINT / DISPLAY).
Real Example: READ Radius / PRINT Area
C Equivalent: scanf("%f", &r); / printf(...)
Process Symbol
Sharp 90° Rectangle
Represents arithmetic operations, data manipulation, or variable assignments. Has exactly one incoming flowline and one outgoing flowline.
Real Example: Area = PI * r * r / count = 0
C Equivalent: float area = 3.14159f * r * r;
Decision Symbol
True 4-Point Rhombus / Diamond
Evaluates a boolean conditional test. Must have one incoming flowline and two distinct outgoing branch flowlines clearly labeled.
Real Example: Is Age >= 18? / Is N == 0?
C Equivalent: if (age >= 18) { ... } else { ... }
On-Page Connector
Exact Circle
Connects converging or distant flowlines on the same page to prevent messy, crisscrossing lines. Contains an identifier letter or number.
Real Example: Convergence junction labeled 1 or A
C Equivalent: Common junction after an if-else block
Predefined Process
Rectangle with Double Vertical Bars
Specifies a call to a separate, modular subroutine or library routine whose detailed flowchart is documented elsewhere.
Real Example: ComputeRoots(a, b, c)
C Equivalent: Calling a function: double r = sqrt(d);

Flowchart Example 1: Pure Sequential Execution

Problem: Calculate the Area and Perimeter of a Rectangle given Length and Width.

Sequential Flow Linear Execution

In a Sequential Flowchart, every instruction executes one after the other in strict linear order from top to bottom with zero branching and zero loops.

Execution Trace Table for Example 1
Step #Flowchart ActionLength (L)Width (W)AreaPerimeterScreen Output
1START-----
2READ Length, Width10.05.0---
3Area = L * W10.05.050.0--
4Perimeter = 2 * (L + W)10.05.050.030.0-
5PRINT Area, Perimeter10.05.050.030.0Area = 50.00, Perimeter = 30.00
6STOP10.05.050.030.0Program terminates cleanly

Flowchart Example 2: Two-Way Selection Decision

Problem: Read two numbers A and B, determine and print the largest number.

Selection Logic True Diamond

In a Selection Flowchart, the control encounters a conditional test inside a Decision Diamond. Control branches into two mutually exclusive paths (TRUE vs FALSE) that subsequently reunite at a connector.

Execution Trace Table for Example 2 (Testing Both Branches)
Test CaseInput AInput BDecision Test (A > B)Branch TakenScreen Output
Case 1251425 > 14 evaluates to TRUEYES branch (Left)A is Largest (25)
Case 27197 > 19 evaluates to FALSENO branch (Right)B is Largest (19)
Case 3 (Equal)121212 > 12 evaluates to FALSENO branch (Right)B is Largest (12)

Flowchart Example 3: Multi-Way Nested Selection (If-Else-If)

Problem: Check if a number N is Positive, Negative, or Zero.

Cascading Diamonds 3-Way Junction

When an algorithm requires choosing among more than two outcomes, decision diamonds are nested or cascaded in sequence:

Execution Trace Table for Example 3
Test Value NDiamond 1: (N > 0)Diamond 2: (N < 0)Final ActionOutput
+42TRUE(Skipped)Prints Positive → Exits to STOPPositive
-15FALSETRUEPrints Negative → Exits to STOPNegative
0FALSEFALSEPrints Zero → Exits to STOPZero

Flowchart Example 4: Iteration / Looping with Loopback Arrow

Problem: Calculate the Sum of First N Natural Numbers (1 + 2 + ... + N).

Cyclic Loop Loopback Arrow

In a Looping Flowchart, instructions execute repeatedly as long as a condition holds True. Notice the Loopback Flowline (cyan dashed line) which travels backward from the bottom of the loop body back to the top of the decision diamond!

Step-by-Step Execution Trace Table for N = 4
CycleLoop Counter (i)Condition (i <= 4)Current SumComputation (Sum + i)New SumNext i (i + 1)
Init1-0-01
Turn 111 <= 4 → TRUE00 + 112
Turn 222 <= 4 → TRUE11 + 233
Turn 333 <= 4 → TRUE33 + 364
Turn 444 <= 4 → TRUE66 + 4105
Exit55 <= 4 → FALSE10Loop Ends!10Prints 10 → STOP

Result: Sum of 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10!

Flowchart Example 5: Sum of Digits of a Number (Slides 42–44)

Curriculum Algorithm: Repeatedly extract rightmost digit using N % 10 and chop using N / 10.

Digit Extraction Slide 42-44

How does a computer sum digits of a number like 1234? It extracts the rightmost digit with modulo 10 (Rem = N % 10), adds it to an accumulator (Sum = Sum + Rem), and truncates the digit with integer division (N = N / 10). It loops until $N$ becomes 0:

Step-by-Step Execution Trace Table for N = 1234
IterationCurrent NRem = N % 10 (Extracted)Sum = Sum + RemNew N = N / 10 (Remaining)
Before Loop1234-01234
Turn 1123440 + 4 = 4123
Turn 212334 + 3 = 712
Turn 31227 + 2 = 91
Turn 4119 + 1 = 100 (Loop Exits!)
Terminated0-10Loop stops; prints 10

Final Output: Sum = 10 (since 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10)!

Complete Solutions to the 6 Practice Challenges (Slide 45)

  1. Sum of Multiples of 3 or 5 below 1000: Loop from 1 to 999. If $(i \% 3 == 0 \lor i \% 5 == 0)$, accumulate $i$ into sum. Answer = 233,168.
  2. Roots of Quadratic Equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$: Calculate discriminant $D = b^2 - 4ac$. If $D > 0$, roots are $\frac{-b \pm \sqrt{D}}{2a}$. If $D == 0$, equal root is $\frac{-b}{2a}$. If $D < 0$, complex roots exist.
  3. Largest of 3 Numbers ($a, b, c$): Compare $a > b$. If true, compare $a > c$ to find max ($a$ or $c$). If false, compare $b > c$ to find max ($b$ or $c$).
  4. Even or Odd: Test if (N % 2 == 0) or bitwise if ((N & 1) == 0) → Even, else Odd.
  5. Quotient and Remainder: In C, A / B performs truncated integer division (quotient), and A % B produces the remainder.
  6. Even Numbers between 100 and 200: Initialize loop variable $i = 102$ and increment with $i = i + 2$ while $i < 200$.

quiz.question: Which flowchart symbol is used to indicate an Input or Output operation (e.g. reading user data or printing a result)?
quiz.explanation: As specified on Slide 33 and ISO 5807, a Parallelogram is the designated symbol for any Input or Output operation.

quiz.question: Which of the following is a mandatory, non-negotiable characteristic of any valid algorithm (Slide 31)?
options: It must be written in the C programming language
It must contain at least 100 lines of code
It must cease execution and terminate after a finite number of steps
It must run inside a graphical user interface
quiz.explanation: Slide 31 states: Finiteness is essential: 'After a specific period, it must cease to run.' An infinite loop cannot be considered an algorithm.

quiz.question: In the Sum of Digits looping algorithm (Slide 42), what operations extract the rightmost digit and discard it?
options: N / 10 to extract, N * 10 to discard
N % 10 to extract, N / 10 to discard
N + 10 to extract, N - 10 to discard
sqrt(N) to extract, log(N) to discard
quiz.explanation: Modulo by 10 (N % 10) yields the remainder (the rightmost digit). Integer division by 10 (N / 10) chops that digit off.

quiz.question: What is the primary advantage of writing pseudocode before converting an algorithm into C code (Slide 32)?
options: Pseudocode compiles directly into assembly instructions
Pseudocode provides structured English close to programming constructs, making translation to code seamless and error-free
Pseudocode replaces the need for a C compiler
quiz.explanation: Slide 32: 'Transforming an algorithm presented in pseudocode to programming code could be much easier than converting an algorithm written in natural language.'

quiz.question: What geometric shape is used in flowcharts to represent a Decision conditional test with multiple exit paths?
quiz.explanation: Slide 33: 'A diamond indicates a point where a decision is made.' It has multiple exit flowlines (e.g. Yes/No or True/False).

quiz.question: What does a small Circle symbol signify in standard ISO flowcharts?
options: An on-page connector used to join converging flowlines without crossing
quiz.explanation: Slide 33: A small circle is an on-page connector indicating where flowlines converge or continue elsewhere on the same page.

title: C Program Structure & GCC Compilation Pipeline
subtitle: The 4-Stage Conveyor Belt: Preprocessor, Compiler, Assembler, Linker
content:
The Software Factory: The 4 Stages of GCC

When you type gcc main.c -o main, your code goes through a 4-station conveyor belt. Here is the visual pipeline:

Source Code Your C Code .c
1. Preprocessor (cpp) Text Expander .i
2. Compiler (cc1) Assembly Gen .s
3. Assembler (as) Object Machine Code .o
4. Linker (ld) Executable Binary .exe / binary

What Each Station Does in Simple Terms

StationTool & GCC CommandWhat It Does in Simple WordsInput → Output
1. Preprocessing gcc -E file.c -o file.i The Text Editor Assistant: Erases all comments (/* */), replaces all #define words with their actual values, and copies the entire content of header files (like stdio.h) directly into your file. .c → .i
2. Compilation gcc -S file.i -o file.s The Blueprint Translator: Checks grammar/syntax rules and translates the clean C code into human-readable Assembly Language. .i → .s
3. Assembly gcc -c file.s -o file.o The Machine Stamper: Translates assembly words into actual binary opcodes (0s and 1s) to produce a relocatable Object File. .s → .o
4. Linking gcc file.o -o file The Puzzle Solver: Merges your object file with precompiled library files (e.g. brings in printf.o from the C runtime library) and creates the final runnable program. .o → Executable
Who Throws What Errors? (Slides 55, 104)

• Syntax Errors: Caught by the Compiler (cc1) during stage 2 (e.g. missing semicolons, misspelled keywords).
• Linker Errors: Caught by the Linker (ld) during stage 4 (e.g. undefined reference to 'main' or undefined reference to 'sqrt' when a function is called but its body cannot be found!).

Transpilers: Source-to-Source Compilers (Slide 61)

A Transpiler takes code written in one high-level language and translates it into another high-level language:

Source LanguageTarget LanguageHistorical Transpiler Name (Slide 61)
C++CCFRONT (Bjarne Stroustrup's original C++ compiler)
C#JavaScriptSCRIPTSHARP
PHPC++HIPHOP for PHP (developed by Facebook for speed)
COBOLCOpen COBOL

quiz.question: Which GCC command line flag stops execution immediately after the Preprocessing phase and outputs preprocessed C code (.i)?
quiz.explanation: As detailed on Slide 52, `gcc -E -o Program1.i Program1.c` runs only the preprocessor, stripping comments and expanding macros/headers into Program1.i.

quiz.question: What is the output artifact generated by the Assembler stage (as / gcc -c)?
quiz.explanation: Slide 53: The assembler (as) translates assembly language instructions into machine language instructions (binary 0 and 1) and generates an object file Program1.o.

quiz.question: If your C program calls printf() from <stdio.h>, which software component is responsible for merging the precompiled printf.o object file with your program's object file?
quiz.explanation: Slide 54: The linker (ld) performs the task of linking object files with external resources (system functions, C runtime libraries like printf.o) to produce the final executable.

quiz.question: According to Slide 61, which historic transpiler was used to convert C++ code into standard C code?
quiz.explanation: Slide 61 lists CFRONT as the transpiler with source language C++ and target language C (originally created by Bjarne Stroustrup).

quiz.question: What is the role of the OS Loader in the program development cycle?
options: It translates assembly language into machine code
It copies the executable program from secondary disk storage into primary memory (RAM) and starts execution
It checks syntax errors in source files
quiz.explanation: Slide 58 specifies phase 5: 'Loader puts program in memory (RAM). CPU takes each instruction and executes it.'

title: Process Memory Layout in C
subtitle: The 5-Story Building Analogy: Text, Data, BSS, Heap, Stack & size Command
content:
The 5-Story Building Analogy (Slide 63)

When you double-click your compiled C program, the Operating System rents an entire building of RAM addresses for your program to live in:

Building FloorMemory SegmentWhat Lives Here in Plain WordsDirection
Top Floor (Penthouse) Arguments & Environment Stores command line arguments (e.g. argc, argv) and OS environment settings. Fixed at Highest Address (~0x7FFF...)
4th Floor Stack Segment The Quick Notepad: Local variables declared inside functions. Fast and automatic! Every time a function is called, a stack frame is created; when the function finishes, everything is automatically tossed in the trash. Grows Downward ↓
Middle Space Unallocated Free RAM Empty space allowing Stack to grow down and Heap to grow up without crashing into each other. -
3rd Floor Heap Segment The Rental Storage Unit: Memory requested manually by you at runtime using malloc(). You are responsible for releasing it with free()! Grows Upward ↑
2nd Floor Uninitialized Data (.bss) Global variables with no starting value (e.g. int a;). Automatically initialized to 0 by the OS kernel. Takes ZERO space in your disk file! Fixed
1st Floor Initialized Data (.data) Global variables with starting values (e.g. int count = 10;) and text string literals. Fixed
Ground Floor / Bedrock Text Segment (Code) The pure machine code instructions executed by the CPU. Marked Read-Only so a buggy program cannot accidentally overwrite its own code! Fixed at Lowest Address (~0x0040...)

The 'size' Command Experiment (Slides 68–69)

The Classroom Demonstration

Slide 68 shows a program with no globals: size Memory.exe → bss = 96.
Slide 69 adds one global: int a; outside main().
Run again: size Memory.exe → bss = 100!
Notice: bss increased by exactly 4 bytes (the size of 1 integer)! Neither text nor data changed!

quiz.question: In which memory segment is an uninitialized global variable (e.g. 'int a;') stored?
quiz.explanation: Slide 65: Uninitialized global and static variables are stored in the uninitialized data segment, historically called the 'bss' (Block Started by Symbol) segment, initialized to 0 by the OS kernel.

quiz.question: What happens in memory when an uninitialized global variable 'int a;' is added to a 32-bit C program, as demonstrated on Slides 68–69?
options: The text segment size increases by 4 bytes
The data segment size increases by 4 bytes
The bss segment size increases by 4 bytes (from 96 to 100)
quiz.explanation: Slides 68–69 demonstrate with the `size` command that adding `int a;` increases only the `bss` column by exactly 4 bytes (96 bytes to 100 bytes).

quiz.question: Why is the Text segment marked as Read-Only in modern operating systems?
options: To prevent running programs from accidentally or maliciously modifying their own instructions
Because hard drives cannot write back to ROM
Because machine code consists only of 0s
quiz.explanation: Slide 64: 'The text segment is often read-only, to prevent a program from accidentally modifying its instructions.'

quiz.question: Which of the following statements about the Stack segment is FALSE?
options: Variables created on the stack are automatically deallocated when they go out of scope
Stack allocation is much faster than heap allocation
The stack grows upward towards higher memory addresses
Infinite recursion can cause a stack overflow
quiz.explanation: Slide 63 & 65 show that the Stack grows DOWNWARD towards lower memory addresses (towards the Heap), while the Heap grows upward.

quiz.question: When should dynamically allocated memory on the Heap be used instead of the Stack?
options: When we need ultra-fast allocation for small integers
When the exact amount of data needed is unknown at compile time and must be allocated on demand at runtime
When writing the main() function definition
quiz.explanation: Slide 67 states: 'We use the heap if we don't know exactly how much data we will need at run time.'
